A two-population Reduced Wong-Wang network has more free connectivity than one empirical functional connectome can pin down, and the tuning workflow of [Schirner et al. (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-38626-y) approaches that in stages. Feedback inhibition control (FIC) adjusts each region's inhibitory weight $J_i$ until excitatory activity sits at its target — a constraint on *activity*, which never looks at the empirical FC at all. The combined FIC+EIB loop adds the long-range and feed-forward-inhibition weights, $w^{LRE}$ and $w^{FFI}$, and scores them against that FC. A gradient fit tunes the same weights through the loss instead of through a hand-written update rule.

All three are declared in the one curated experiment this page references, and all three write into one container, so what follows compares them on the numbers the run produced rather than on three separate scripts.

Everything below is declared in [`EI_Tuning_tvboptim.yaml`](EI_Tuning_tvboptim.yaml). The page runs that recipe and shows what it produced; it contains no plotting code and no analysis of its own.

## The recipe

```yaml
experiments:
    - tvbo:experiment/EI_Tuning_FIC_EIB_Optimization
```

An algorithm declares what it tracks, and that declaration is what puts the loop's own history in the container:

```yaml
algorithms:
  fic_eib:
    depends_on: [fic]
    observations: [mean_S_e, mean_S_i, bold, fc_inloop, fc_target]
    update_rules:
      - name: wLRE_update
        target_parameter: {name: wLRE}
        equation:
          rhs: "wLRE[i,k] + eta * (fc_target[i,k] - fc_inloop[i,k]) * sqrt(...)"
```

## Run it

```{python}
from tvbo import SimulationStudy

study = SimulationStudy.from_file("EI_Tuning_tvboptim.yaml")
results = study.run(root="../_build/EI_Tuning_tvboptim")
results
```

## The containers

The container comes back in the shape the recipe declares it in. `algorithms.fic_eib.history` is the loop's tracked set, one record per iteration; the per-region and per-edge quantities keep their region axes, so a weight matrix is selected by region name rather than by an index you have to trust.

```{python}
results["exp-3"].algorithms.fic_eib.history
```

Every group inherits the run's coordinates from the root, so selecting a region works the same way at any depth:

```{python}
results["exp-3"].algorithms.fic_eib.history["J_i"].sel(node=["L.SFG", "R.SFG"])
```

## Result

```{python}
#| echo: false
results.figure()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(results.figure().caption)
```

FIC does what it is asked: mean excitatory gating falls from $0.41$ to $0.23$ against a target of $0.25$ **(a)**. That is a statement about activity, and it buys almost nothing in FC — the resulting correlation with the empirical matrix is $0.18$ **(e)**, which is what a constraint that never sees the target should be expected to give.

Two numbers in **(b)** are worth keeping apart. The in-loop correlation the FIC+EIB loop tracks climbs from $0.13$ to $0.49$, but that is `fc_inloop`, computed on the loop's sliding window with no skip beyond the settle. Re-evaluated afterwards on a fresh simulation with the recipe's declared $20$-TR skip, the same fit scores $0.26$ **(f)**. The recipe declares those as two observations precisely because they are two quantities; the loop's own score is the optimistic one, and reading it as the fit's quality would overstate this fit by roughly a factor of two.

The gradient fit reaches $0.84$ on that same clean re-evaluation, with the combined loss falling from $0.32$ to $0.09$ **(c)**. Both routes end up tuning the same two weight matrices, **(g)** and **(h)**, which are the study's actual deliverable: per-edge long-range excitation and feed-forward inhibition, on labelled region axes.
